items.q: What does Big-O notation actually describe?
options: How the amount of work grows as the input size grows
How much memory your computer has
The exact number of seconds an algorithm takes

explain.right: Big-O describes growth: how the number of steps scales as input size n increases, ignoring constants and hardware.
explain.wrong: It is not a measurement in seconds, not your RAM size, and not about the language; it's a growth rate.

items.q: Order these from best (slowest-growing) to worst as n gets large:

explain.right: Constant beats logarithmic beats linear beats quadratic: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n^2) by growth.
explain.wrong: The other orderings scramble the classes; they do not grow the same (the gaps are enormous at large n).

items.q: A friend says 'O(n^2) means the program takes n-squared seconds.' Why is that wrong?
options: It should be n-squared minutes, not seconds
O(n^2) actually means it never finishes
Big-O drops constants and units; it describes how runtime scales with n, not a clock time

explain.right: Big-O strips out constants and units to capture growth shape; it tells you doubling n roughly quadruples the work, not any specific second count.
explain.wrong: It's not a unit of time at all, and O(n^2) finishes fine; the error is treating a growth rate as a stopwatch reading.

items.q: A function has a loop over all n items, and inside it another loop over all n items. Its time complexity is about:

explain.right: Nested loops each running n times do about n x n = n^2 steps, so it's O(n^2).
explain.wrong: O(1)/O(log n)/O(n) describe no-loop, halving, and single-pass work respectively; two nested full passes square the work.

items.q: Why can an O(n^2) algorithm sometimes beat an O(n log n) one in practice?
rubric: Big-O ignores constant factors and lower-order terms
For small n, those hidden constants can dominate, so the 'worse' class may run faster
Big-O matters most as n gets large / describes scaling, not small-input speed

explain.right: Good answers note Big-O hides constants, so on small inputs a simpler O(n^2) can win; the asymptotic advantage shows up as n grows.
explain.wrong: A weak answer claims Big-O is always decisive, ignoring that constants and input size matter for real runtime.
